utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Mladen Naletilic and Vinko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, everybody, and welcome back to this case. I notice Mr. Stringer is here. It has been a long time. Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Thank you, and it's good to be back. I'll be -- I think the Trial Chamber has received a letter from Mr. Scott. I'll be standing in for him this week but I will be staying with the case until its conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are so glad to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: On the 2nd of August this year, this Trial Chamber made a decision for the videolink conference this week. We will hear eight witnesses in five days so there are specific time limits for each witness. Next Monday, we will hear another witness for Martinovic's case through the videolink, and after that, we will hear directly a witness in Naletilic's case on Tuesday, September the 3rd, 2002, in The Hague. In the meantime, I would like to remind both parties that this case should be completed by 27th September, 2002. As for the time schedule, we will have four sittings today. Each will last for one hour to an hour and 30 minutes, between which we will have three breaks. Now -- yes? Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of the Defence, thank you for your words of welcome, and I'd also like to say good morning to my learned friends. Your Honours, unfortunately, I'm faced with major problems with witnesses who were to testify by videolink, but could we go into private session so that I could tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in open session. Are there any protective measures for the first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. As before, distortion and a pseudonym, that is all, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure that we are talking about witness number 2 on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We have no objections to the protective measures, Mr. President. Mr. Bos will be involved with that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I was informed that the facial distortion and the pseudonym, the facial distortion -- I mean the image will not be broadcast outside but we will see the image on our screen. So your request for the protective measures is granted. Could we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Hello?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, will you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me and see me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krsnik. I can see you and hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let us start with our work. Kindly -- the Registrar is going to show you a piece of paper with your name. Please don't say your name. Just say yes if this is indeed your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe we could go into private session. I don't know whether this can be heard outside. We want to hear some personal data from this witness. Maybe we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My next question is as follows: If it indeed happened that somebody was taken away from the hospital or from any other medical institution to the Heliodrom, would you have learned about that at the Heliodrom? Did you know exactly how many people there were there, and would you have learned that if something like that had happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Most probably I would have, for a simple reason: Doctors who worked there had the possibility to communicate with me directly, because Croatian doctors could telephone me, could -- and I personally made visits, made rounds of the centre, and I tried to notice any change, any inhumane treatment. It was my task to notice that, in time, try to deal with that, either personally or with the help of Dr. Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, can you please tell the Honourable Court everything you know about the Heliodrom? We've heard stories here, all sorts of different stories. I would kindly ask you to tell us about the Heliodrom. That's why you are here. At the beginning of my case, I said that the Defence would present all the possible evidence, and I believe that your testimony is one of those testimonies that will clarify to the Honourable Court the situation in the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: The Heliodrom was, for me personally, a very unpleasant life experience. However, having said that, I have to say that I'm very proud of what I did there, because I believe that as a doctor, despite all the difficulties that I saw there, I did so much, and at the end of the day, no epidemic was registered. Whatever causes of epidemics could be there, I tried to spot them, to prevent them. As I am a professional and expert, I found it much easier to notice the potential foci of epidemics. Further on, I educated other doctors and taught them how to do their job, because I must tell you that the military epidemiology is not taught at any university because in the ex-Yugoslavia there were no military medical schools, and I gathered my experience when I was working in the JNA, and I selflessly shared my knowledge. Can you please ask me specific questions? A lot of time has gone by, and can you ask me some specific questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: First of all, did you control food? Do you know how they were fed? That will be my first question. Second question: Did they have an outpatient surgery? Who were the doctors who were working there all the time in the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: As far as the food there is concerned, in May 1993 there was still a lack of food. There was still not enough food. For example, my children were refugees and they did not have enough food. But I did, on my part, with the help of Dr. Bagaric and who turned to other people, I did all I could to provide people with food. Secondly, all the people who distributed food and who had to work with food had to be previously tested for germs. What does that mean? That means that somebody may have been contagious and could have contaminated the food. In order to prevent that, we examined all those who got in touch with the food, and that's how we prevented the outbreak of any epidemics. Thirdly, whatever food was given to the people was controlled on a sample. The sample was kept in a fridge. There was a book in which the data were recorded every day on what was -- what food was given to the people. So the data was recorded on breakfast, lunch, and dinner, who was the chef, what was cooked, who controlled the food, and this was signed by the person in charge of that. So as far as the food is concerned, at the beginning the food was bad, and that's for sure. However, as the number of men went down, the food improved, gradually. And I can say for a fact that at one point in time the food that was given to the inmates was the same food that was given to their guards, the Home Guards, who were providing security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let's stop here just for a second, please. Let's just clarify some things. You said, if I have understood you well, in your own words, you said that, and if I have understood you well, you said that that food was given to everybody in the Heliodrom: to the soldiers, inmates, and to those who provided security. Did I understand you well? Did you really say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Basically, yes. Perhaps not in the early days, but later on, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Be so kind. We are talking about security now. Do you know what kind of security was it, who guarded the Heliodrom? Could everybody enter this Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: No, not everybody was admitted there. I had a special permit, and there was the military police, and they controlled and checked the identity of everybody. And personally, perhaps nothing to do with your question, but I delivered two or three lectures to members of the military police related to the Geneva Conventions. Because as a man, as a physician, as a humanist - excuse me. I'm slightly emotional - I was afraid of revenge, because there were people who were wounded. And I delivered those lectures mostly to those men, and I think that that is, well, a kind of my contribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Doctor, thank you very much for your explanation, although it has nothing to do with my question. But did you personally observe any harassment at the Heliodrom by those men who guarded it or by somebody else? Did any detainees complain to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Since in the town of Mostar --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mind that you don't reveal your identity. If need be, we shall go back into private session, but just take care. Shall we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So were those military? Were they civilians? What do you know about them? If you do know anything about it, will you please tell the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know any definite number, and if I said something exact, I don't know, but I think that an approximate number could be, I don't know, 1200, 1300, 1500. It's difficult to say. You know, it's difficult really, difficult to say. As for people whom I met there, I didn't know a number -- a majority of them. Those I did know were Mostarans, that is my townsmen, people that I knew from before. But they were but few. I also know that already sometime in late May, their number drastically decreased and continued to drop. So that I think that in 1994, in the beginning of 1994, I think there were much -- very few people, only perhaps a few hundred. And the conditions of course were much better, but these are only approximate figures. I will repeat, 1200, 1300, 1500, not more than that, during this most deplorable period and later on, 200, 300, 400, 500. So these figures are not particularly reliable, but that is what I can give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, doctor, this is also helpful. Do you perhaps know what was the situation towards the end of the summer, and when did the number begin to decrease? You said that there were never more than 1500, if I understood you well. Do you know when did this number begin to drop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Well, you see, sometime after ten or 15 days, the number drastically dropped. Why, I don't know. Nobody told me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Nor did I ask for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm asking only what you personally know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I know that a number drastically dropped because I knew indirectly, and I will mention the JNA because there are certain things that you can learn indirectly on the basis of the number of meals. That is how you can get some impression. And I'm telling you, as the summer came to a close, as the delegations came, international, Bosniak and Croat, I suppose, some exchanges took place or something, something at a political level, and then the number was smaller. And to us, or specifically for me, it became much easier to work because it is of course much easier to take care of a smaller number of people than of a larger number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did you also take care or are you aware that there were at the Heliodrom some detained Croats, for different reasons? Were you aware of them and did you look after them, or was it somebody else's responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Let me tell you, of course there were Croats there, surely, because I knew some of them. And I tell you again, I'm a doctor, I cannot discriminate for or against him because he's a Croat, give him something better or something worse because he's not a Croat. He got what we had, and what we could administer to him as quickly as possible and as best as possible, because you see, the team that treated -- there was the team headed by Gagic who was for the prevention of diseases, and there was also a team which provided us with medication, so it was, let me say, a system, a system which worked for the sake of normalcy and with a view to improving things. If you -- you can treat patients but if you apply prophylactic measures you also preventively treat them. So all the medical supplies that we had, we distributed them not according whether this one was this or this one was that, but only to the patients who needed them most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And my last two questions, Witness. Can you tell us, if you know, that is, whether you personally talked with those people and what did they tell you, why were they there? So what is it that you know about it? That would be my penultimate question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Well, you see, I talked. Among others, there were people who were members of the BH Army. Supposedly this was being taken care by the -- by the military investigative body, but I'm not interested in that because I'm a doctor. I'm interested in men. And sometimes I would ask, "Why is he here?" And they would say, "He's suspected of this or that." And others were isolated as a preventive measure. That is what I was told, because when this unfortunate war started in Mostar and Mostar is a multi-ethnic town, and there were tenants of different ethnic origins or faiths in buildings, and there was perhaps a danger that a neighbour would attack a neighbour. Perhaps this was a kind of an excuse, even though I don't really think that people are all that mean, but perhaps the politicians do think that, and that is why they called it a centre for preventive isolation. But I'm telling you, some ten days ago I was on the left bank, that is in the Bosniak part, with a colleague of mine, and people who were there for, say, Stranjak, we are still friends, because we realised that it was evil that he did not ask for, that I did not ask for, that it was evil but we were people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And my last question, Witness, will be: Where were you on the 9th of May, 1993? Tell us something about your personal experience, if you have any, that is, and in relation to this penultimate question, can you, approximately, of course, tell us how many Mostarans were there in -- at the Heliodrom and how many were those who came from elsewhere? Can you give us any figure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: It is very difficult, you know. I used to be a sports physician once upon a time, and when I would read reports from matches, I would compare the number of people present at the match with the figure in the newspaper, so I gained some impressions of mine, but again it is very difficult. You understand -- you have to understand, I am a physician. Any -- every time that somebody came there, it was a stress. It is still a stress when I have a patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, doctor. If you can tell us, tell us. If you can't, never mind. Just approximately, just to give us some idea?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Well, perhaps, perhaps, I don't know, if I see ten people, I know two or three of them. Others, I don't. Or I join a group, there are ten of them, I don't know anyone, or I join a group of five, I know them all. But perhaps I knew about 20 or 30 per cent of people, and those were people who are even my friends, who in (redacted) (redacted), don't go to the left bank. Nobody -- none of us will do anything to you but there are some other people there, some outsiders, some refugees, and they might do something." And that is the thing that I also told to my friends on the right bank, because you know a war is an abnormal situation, there are emotions which surface, which you cannot keep under control. So my figure would be 20, 30 per cent, but don't really take it as gospel because I'm really making pure guesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Well, tell us, do you know something about the date of the 9th of May, 1993? Where were you, if you were anywhere, what you saw, if you saw anything? What do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Well, you see, in my life, there are several very unpleasant dates, dates that I will never forget, and perhaps that is my post-traumatic syndrome, but you see, I was in my -- in my flat, and I was asleep, and the gun-fire started. I was taken aback. I mean, in every organised army you are supposed to know what is about to happen, but I didn't know anything and there was shooting and shooting and shooting. After a while, my telephone rang. At that moment I had a privilege, I had an army telephone, and they told me that an attack had started and that I had to get to the main medical staff without delay, and it was several kilometres away from my house. I had an official vehicle. I couldn't get the driver because the gun-fire was frightening, and about 100 or 200 metres as the crow flies from me, there was a sniper firing. It is where the seat or the headquarters of the ABiH Army unit was, the White Corps or whatever it was called. I couldn't really leave the house all that easily. Across the street from me, there is the civilian police, so I called them. They came. I was downstairs. They stopped right at the front door. I entered the Golf. I lay down, and then a part of the road, that is for about 20 metres, we covered so fast, and I arrived safely to the main medical -- to the main medical headquarters where I stayed several days, never leaving the building. We were getting the food from the hospital. But I'm telling you one of the worst moments in my life was that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you said the attack started. Whose attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Well, I was told that it was the BH Army which had launched the attack. "Mind you don't take this street because there is a sniper. You'll be killed." And I looked from under the blinds, and in neither street was there a single person. This situation was sad, the situation was impossible. There was this horrible odour, and I realised that a human head was worth nothing, because it wouldn't survive, because there were snipers on both sides. And I can affirm that there was fire opened from Vranica, and there are still bullet marks in my building, and I was told that at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And who fired from Vranica at your building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Well, they were not firing at my flat. There was simply fire. Well, that is the building where the command of the -- I believe the 4th Corps from Mostar was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, thank you very much. I have no further questions for you. Thank you very much for coming and thank you for making the effort and finding time to come and help us with your testimony. And now I will hand you over to my learned friend. Thank you very much once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honours, as I see, it is now time for the break. It is 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it is time for a break. I hope during the break the LiveNote on the small computer could be fixed. We'll rise until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since we have few witnesses for the videolink conference, so we won't sit very late today. I think we'll finish today's sitting at 4.00. And after 4.00, the acting Senior Legal Officer will approach both parties for some procedural matters. Well, Mr. Bos, are you ready for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have any document to furnish to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we've provided the court deputy with a bundle of documents which we are using in cross-examination, and I hope that the witness in Zagreb will also have the documents in Zagreb. They were given to the court deputy in Zagreb, so they should be also in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness NU. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We don't hear the witness, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, we don't hear you. You may hear us, but we don't hear you, so I think there is a technical problem. Witness, could you -- if you hear me, could you again say something so that we can see if we can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you appear to be hearing us, but we don't hear you, so I think something needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I was told that we need a few minutes, the technicians, to check it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can you hear us, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos. It seems everything is okay. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. We can hear you now as well. Witness, my name is Mr. Roeland Bos, from the Office of the Prosecution, and I will ask you some questions in cross-examination. Witness, I'll start off with my first question. You've testified that you worked at the Mostar hospital during the war in 1993. What I would like to ask you: What is the size of the hospital? If you compare it to the other hospitals in Mostar, would this be the biggest hospital in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: In Mostar, on the right bank, there is just one hospital, which at the time was called the War Hospital. The department at which I was on call and occasionally worked was the Department for Contagious Diseases of the War Hospital. So to answer your question, on the right bank there is just one hospital, which may have several buildings, but there was only one hospital, which at the time was called the War Hospital in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And during the war in 1993, how many patients, on average, would be hospitalised on a daily basis? What was the capacity of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Sir, Your Honours, I was there on call, because I was engaged in the HVO, and since there were not enough specialists for contagious diseases - there were three with me, four altogether - I was on call to provide professional help. At the time, my department consisted of not more than ten beds, and as far as the capacity of the hospital, you should ask the principal of the War Hospital and Mr. Bagaric, who was the chief of the medical corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But could you give us a rough estimation on the number of beds of the hospital? Are we talking about hundreds of beds, thousands of beds, dozens of beds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: In my department, I had 10 or 11 beds. That department was relocated to the Department of Internal Diseases, because my former department, the Department for Contagious Diseases, was given to psychiatry. Namely, when the Serbian army, the Army of Republika Srpska, and the JNA, chased psychiatry from Domanovici, these patients sought asylum partly in my department and partly in ATD in Mostar. So the number of beds may have been hundreds of them, but I don't know the exact number. There were no -- certainly not a thousand beds. Not even today does that hospital have a thousand beds, but there were several hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you spoke about the number of detainees at the Heliodrom, and you were asked to give an estimation on the number of detainees, and while you estimated that in May, there were about 1200, maybe at the most 1500 detainees but that number dramatically dropped after ten days. Witness, if I put it to you that in August, 1993, there were about -- there were over 2.000 detainees at the Heliodrom, what would you say to that? Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I don't think it would be possible because what I saw with my colleagues who took me there does not corroborate this figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I will ask now the Court deputy who is there with you to show you an exhibit, which is Exhibit number P565.04. And I would like to you read it. And it's a letter from Mr. Stanko Bozic, and let me first ask you, do you know who Mr. Stanko Bozic is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Yes. I met Mr. Bozic because I helped him in a certain way, but I see this letter for the first time, and never did Mr. Bozic give anything similar to me, never did he enable me to see this figure, and I cannot corroborate this figure. I know Mr. Bozic, but I see this for the first time in my life. Because you can see who this letter was sent to, to Mr. Stojic, to Mr. Coric, and to the archives, so I don't know how would I be able to know anything about this, not having seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, let me explain to you why I'm showing you this letter. This letter is a letter signed by Mr. Bozic who is the -- who was the warden of the Heliodrom in 1993, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I assume -- I can see the stamps. I assume this is correct. I assume this is his signature. However, you yourself can see that this was never sent to the Medical Corps, more specifically to Dr. Bagaric, and even if this had been sent to him --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm not claiming it was sent to the Medical Corps. I'm just using this exhibit to show you at the second paragraph where Mr. Bozic, who is the warden of the Heliodrom, talks about the fact that there were 2100 detainees at the Heliodrom. Is it correct that that's what this letter says? And isn't it correct that Mr. Bozic would know this much better than you would?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Bozic was the warden, which is confirmed by his signature. I said that the military police provided security, and obviously he should have known -- have had more information. But I must tell you also that I was taken to the detainees by my colleagues, doctors, and what I saw, I gave you just approximate figures. I found everything shocking. Whether this is correct, I do not know, but the figure that I gave you was based on my insight. If that figure is not correct, then Mr. Bozic did not take me to some parts of the detention centre because maybe my assistance was not needed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But wouldn't you agree with me that Mr. Bozic was in a better position to assess the number of detainees than you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Obviously, if he was the warden, it is only logical that he should have known better than me, but I again tell you that I don't know why he did not inform me about that, because on several occasions he asked for my assistance. So I don't know why I wasn't informed. I see this figure, Your Honours, for the first time, and I hear this information for the first time in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, Witness, is it correct that in the autumn of 1993, that during that period, you not only visited the Heliodrom but you also visited other detention centres, like Gabela, Ljubuski and Livno, and that you sort of inspected these detention centres and that you actually issued reports on the conditions of these detention centres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: You probably remember that I, at the beginning of -- said that when I left the JNA, I was a professional who was familiar not only with medical profession but with the military epidemiology and that I was very soon promoted, but I also told you that upon the order of Dr. Bagaric, I was supposed to go to these centres and to act according to the principles of humanity and to teach my colleagues. I also told you that at no school of medicine in the former Yugoslavia these things are not taught, and my superior, Dr. Bagaric, told me, "You are a doctor who knows these things, and you should help. If you need assistance, you can always come to me. This is a shame on all of us and we have to do everything possible to put things right."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, if I understand your question [sic] you say that you were ordered by Mr. Bagaric to do this, and one of the things he asked you was to teach at the detention centres issues of international humanitarian law. Now, is it correct that Mr. Bagaric asked you to do this after the Red Cross had visited the Heliodrom on the 10, 11 and 12 of August, 1993 and had concluded that there were breaches of the Geneva Conventions in this -- in the Heliodrom, for three different reasons: one, because the detainees were taken out for labour; two, because the quality and the quantity of the food was insufficient; and three, because the isolation cells were in bad condition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we have some arguments from my learned friend where does his knowledge come from? Where does he draw his knowledge in order to be able to ask this question in his cross? And where is that document provided by the Red Cross, in which it says this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos, lay some background on those allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will come to that later on with some of the exhibits I will use, but for now I would just like to pose this question to the witness, but this will come back in one of the exhibits which I will use later on. So if you allow me to continue and have this witness respond to this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think you have to lead this witness step by step. First you have to ask this witness whether he's aware of the visit by the Red Cross on a certain time. Then later on, you could follow up your other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, were you aware that the Red Cross visited the Heliodrom mid-August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I heard that the -- indirectly, because my duty was to prevent contagious diseases and education of my colleagues. I know that Mr. Loncar, Dr. Loncar, from the International Red Cross was also involved and Dr. Bagaric had contacts with him. I heard that as hearsay from them, but directly I was not involved. Whenever I asked for information, I would receive it, and it was our intention, and Dr. Bagaric always said, "Everything has to be made available to the international organisations, the international laws have to be respected, humanitarian laws have to be respected, and medicine should be our guiding principle, the principles of medicine should be our guiding principles."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you were aware that the Red Cross visited the Heliodrom in August, 1993, do you also know what their conclusions were after their inspection visit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: No. I did not have any information. The information I had was -- I always wrote reports, a lot of reports, and I knew that the war had started, that it would go on, and that it would eventually finish, that there would be different statements, some more credible, some less credible, some even false statements. That is why I documented everything, in order to be able to remember everything I did, the ways I acted. And Dr. Bagaric always told us to involve all the authorities and that all the situations which proved to be inhumane and which were against human rights should be reported. In addition to that, Dr. Bagaric provided me with information that he considered he should provide me with, some people in charge of the hospital, some of the patients, some of the medicines, and he gave me information pertaining to my area. And I also exchanged information with him, but he very often consulted me on various methods and sought my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But, Witness, the only thing I would like to know now is that all your activities with regard to the detention centres and the reports you drafted on these detention centres, were they all after the Red Cross had visited the Heliodrom in August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first time I visited Heliodrom was on the 11th and 12th of May, 1993. Doctors who were there, when they saw the detainees, they did not know what to do, so Dr. Bagaric sent me urgently to educate my colleagues. So our work started long before. I'm sure you have my report from 11 and 12 May in which it says we educated these people, but not only them. Until the beginning of the conflict with Muslims, I educated my colleagues, Muslims, Bosniaks, because I thought we would be in this together. So it was not on Bagaric's order or on the orders of the Red Cross that I went there. I just went there because Bagaric told me, "Go there because this is what happened and see what you can do to help."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But isn't it correct - and we will come to those reports - that you issued several reports on various camps in the autumn of 1993, especially in November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I assume that it was so. I was the person with the highest authority in the area of prevention and the Geneva Conventions. I don't know how things are in your country but in the former Yugoslavia, these things are not taught at schools. This is the experience I gathered in the army, when I was studying to become a major, and my superior, Dr. Bagaric, thought that I was the best prepared to go there and that he is the person who can put things right if necessary. And wherever I went, I went to alleviate human suffering.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you -- you've been answering my questions very elaborately, and I'm going to ask -- my questions have been quite simple, and several of them could have been answered by yes or no. But your answers are very elaborate, and I'm going to ask you to be a bit more concise and listen to the question and just answer the question which I ask you. Now, Witness, I'm going to show you another exhibit, which is Exhibit P618.1, and I hope that the court deputy could give you that document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And my question is: Witness, could you look at this report, and is it correct -- this is a report dated 30 September, 1993, on the conditions in the Heliodrom. And is it correct that you issued and drafted this report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: The date, yes, the 30th of September. I remember the date. Now, who drew up this report, I'm not sure. I don't really think it was me, simply because if you look at my reports, you will see that there is always to the side "H/C." But I'm sure that this is a correct report. Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: On the last page of the report -- in fact, you co-signed it with two other doctors, but is it correct that on the last page of the report, your signature appears as one of the members of this commission who reported on the conditions in September at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Yes, I am one of the co-signatories, and you will also see that Dr. Kolak and Dr. Sandrk are members of the main medical staff. And sure, I was on the team. Because you have to understand that among other things, I had a team for emergency interventions. If there was an -- if an epidemiological incident broke out somewhere, then I would go there with the team. I wasn't on the member of the staff to sit at the headquarters. I was in the field, to go there and alleviate troubles. But I am a co-signatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, if you have a closer look at the report, and I'll highlight a few of the things that were established in this report. Under number 3 on the first page of the report, it says that the - this concerns the Heliodrom - that the centre's surroundings and the centre itself are messy and neglected. Under number 4, it says that the centre is overcrowded with inmates. Under number 8, it says the hygienic conditions are absolutely unsatisfactory and there is a great likelihood of an outbreak of intestinal and respiratory diseases. And under 7, that there is no segregation in the centre between the wounded, the sick, and the healthy inmates. Is it correct that those were some of the findings in this report, Witness NU?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Your Honours, if it is written, then it must be correct. But let me tell you: If you came to Mostar now, you would see that it's absolutely dirty, and the television and the press keep writing about this. I am an expert of the WHO, and I frequently appeared on television in Mostar saying that because of the situation such as it is, an epidemic is likely to break out, and at any time, under 3. I'm also glad that you can see, under number 5, what I said about medicines. About number 7, I do not know what is not clear there. There is no segregation. We are not segregating people. We are not separating them under any basis. I suppose you have some friends who are physicians, and you will understand that there is no segregation, because segregation equals discrimination in Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 14675 to 14678. our mind. And what else did you say? I believe you mentioned number 8. Well, you see, the number of people must have been larger, but they were leaving, as I already said. And it is a fact that if there is a large number of people in one place, then either respiratory or intestinal diseases are likely to appear. And that is why the literature said that the first thing you must pay attention to is to reduce the number of people as much as possible in order to reduce the risk of disease. At any rate, in any hospital of the world, you have the -- infections will always spread, even in a family, when you have a larger family. It is less likely to spread in a household where there are less people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, in the report you give seven proposed measures. My question is: Were all these measures that you proposed actually followed up after this report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: First let me explain something. Dr. Bagaric heard my proposal. I don't remember the exact date. And then he wrote that the work at the centre for the preventive insulation, as we called it, was the priority task, and that physicians working in home guard units were responsible for it and the administrators, such as Mr. Bozic, was responsible, and the higher institutions were to ensure this. And I suppose you listened to what I was saying, and if a patient clinic was set up, an infirmary was set up, there were medicines, and there is no doubt that severe wounded were taken to Mostar, if possible, if there were any. And I can even tell you that at night-time and at times I had difficulties with drivers, drivers who had to take people to the War Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. I'll leave this exhibit. I'll ask you now to look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course the document speaks for itself, but I'm really bothered by something. Look at what the gentlemen from the Prosecution wrote in the document description for this document. They wrote here -- this list that they gave you, they say that this report was written to avoid embarrassment in view of the expected ICRC inspection. Where does the document say that and where does this transpire from? I think this is absolutely inadmissible and cannot be done. And this is not the first time, except that perhaps I sometimes fail to mention it. But it does not transpire anywhere, either from the English or from the Croatian text. Unfortunately, it is not the first time for the Prosecutor to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, that is a good point. We would like to hear some explanations from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, the description of the exhibit is not the evidence. I mean, the evidence is in. We show the document and -- so as far as the Prosecution is concerned, Your Honours can read the document and assess what the document is about. And if the description is inaccurate, so be it, but the document is in there as well. So it's not that we try to mislead the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed, but be careful with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like you now to look at five exhibits, and four of them are reports on the Heliodrom, on Gabela, Livno, Ljubuski, and one is a chart, an overall chart, on the overall conditions of these four centres. And the exhibits I'd like you to look at are P686.2, which is the chart; and then Exhibit P698.1, which is the report on the Heliodrom; P699.1, which is the report on Gabela; P700.2, which is the report on Livno; and P702.2, which is the report on Ljubuski. Witness, there are a lot of documents which are going to be shown to you now, and I basically ask you to glance through them and confirm to us that you actually drafted these reports or actually -- or indeed signed these reports. Could you please do that and then I'll ask some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honours, but the witness should first read those reports to properly confirm the contents and the signature. So could he be given some time to read them so that he can give valid answers to my learned friend? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think so, because Mr. Bos said that "I basically asked you to glance through them and confirm to us that you actually drafted those reports," so the witness should have time to read those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry, but while the witness is reading, let us try to resolve under dilemma while we are waiting for him. I'm very curious and very -- and I ask Your Honours about the source of this document. It says here that it is the Croatian government, and I affirm publicly in this courtroom that it cannot be the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you have a chance to challenge the authenticity of this document by asking some questions about the sources of this document, but first of all we would like to hear whether this witness has signed this document himself or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are so many documents. I'd need at least a few hours to read them. So I merely look at the signatures. Yes, this is my signature, indicating also the duty I held, and from it you can see that it's mostly the prevention. I just looked at it quickly. Yes, this is my signature, as far as signatures is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... exhibit you just looked at, the number, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Give me a better copy. 1-164/93, of the 30th of November, 1993, P702.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, on the top page of each exhibit, on the English version at least, there is -- there appears an exhibit number in the right-hand corner, and that's the number I need to know. And maybe the Court deputy can assist, can assist in giving me the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The exhibit number that he is looking at this moment is P702.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: This exhibit, is it correct, Witness, that this is an exhibit, this is a report on Ljubuski and that you actually signed this report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: The signature is mine. Now I look at other people who did the round with me, Srecko Tomic, yes, that's a person from Ljubuski, yes, it has to do with Ljubuski. Yes, please. It is my signature and it is Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And is it indeed your report on Ljubuski or would you need more time to read it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, of course I need it. The signature is mine, the number, yes, no question about it, but let me have a look. If you want me to comment on every specific item, perhaps it would be better. Shall I comment on them?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, no, Witness, I don't want you to comment on them. I'm just asking you whether this was the report that you issued on Ljubuski. That's my simple question, and you can just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Yes, I said so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I have already told you so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You can leave that report aside and that's the only information I need to know from you on this report. And maybe the Court deputy can give you now the next exhibit. Maybe let's go one by one. If the witness could be shown P700.2, and the same question applies here, Witness. Is that your signature at the end of the last page of the report, and is it indeed your report on the detention centre in Livno?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, this is unquestionably my signature. Now, when I look at people who were together with me, yes, it is definitely Livno. But if I may, just one sentence, this is yet another proof that I, as a person, knew that sooner or later, time would come when everything would fall in its place and that there would be such an institution of high moral qualities and high professional skills such as you who would finally tell us the truth, because unfortunately, there is a thousand and one truths to this day, and I shall be very happy when the real truth is known.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Then could you look at the next exhibit, which is P699.1? And again, is it your report on the Gabela camp, and is it your signature at the last page of the report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: The signature is unquestionably mine. The beginning here is very poorly copied, but it's Gabela, yes, I can see that, and I can see some of the fellow doctors, yes, people who worked there, or this regiment, Knez Domagoj and yes, I know that they worked in Gabela.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you could now look at Exhibit P6 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Bos, can I ask a question now? Maybe you know the answer or maybe the witness does, but when we are looking at the reports in relation to the conditions in the various detention centres, a distinction seems to be made between a ward and a detainee. Could you clarify that just for my curiosity? At first I thought it was a bad translation of a warden or a warder, but it's clearly somebody who is kept at the Heliodrom. Could you deal with that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I actually came across the same question in preparing this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, in some of the reports, you're referring to the term "ward," and from the context it seems that using the term "ward" is referring to a detainee, but is there a difference between a ward and a prisoner or a ward and a detainee? Could you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Well, you see, the term that I heard from Professor Lang [phoen] for the centre for preventive isolation, a ward or a detainee, was to me, if I look at him from the medical point of view, was a man who was sick or a man who was healthy. I did not care, as a doctor, into which category he was placed by you or somebody else. My question was how to help him not to fall ill, how to help him get well, how to enable him to leave that place as quickly as possible. And to talk about categories to me, as a doctor, that is incompatible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So if I understand your answer correctly, for you there is no distinction between a ward and a detainee?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: No. Allow me. For me there is only a person who happens to be there, who needs treatment, or who needs to be given, or the environment or food or something, so that he doesn't fall ill. I wouldn't call him either this or that. It's a man in need, a man in distress, a man who has been badly traumatised, mentally or otherwise, and I'm there to help him either by prevention or by supplying therapy for him or using psychological treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, do you still have Exhibit P699.1 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Yes. The lady is looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I think one of the reasons why Her Honour raised this question, if you go under item number 3, which is in your version the third page, the B/C/S version, you talk about the accommodation of wards and detainees. Now, in understanding your answers, would the difference between a ward and a detainee be that a ward is somebody who is either physically or mentally ill and a detainee isn't? Or could you please clarify that to us again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Let me tell you, it is the same. In principle, it is the same, that is a ward or a detainee. It's the same. Because I, as a doctor, or any one of us cannot know under such -- under which conditions he's there until he comes to you as a sick or a healthy person. So it's the same. The term is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps -- perhaps I might join. In the Croatian original, it says, " sticenika-uhicenika" that is "ward-detainee." There is no the word "and," there is no connective. And my colleague says in English there is no the word "and." It is not "wards and detainees," but "wards-detainees." So grammatically and linguistically, it falls into the same category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, it may say "wards-detainees" on the introduction to the paragraph, but in the narrative it uses the word "and" rather than "dash." And I was wondering -- perhaps the doctor could hear my question: I was wondering if a distinction was made between somebody who was a ward, who was kept in the Heliodrom allegedly as a preventive measure and somebody who was held in the Heliodrom because he was a member of the Armija. Would he be aware of that? Was that why there was a distinction? In other words, some people were soldiers and some were civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Clark, if you look at the second page, where it says, "Nutrition" or "Diet," you will see, "Wards-detainees are getting everything that is necessary." And as I have said, as Mr. Krsnik has said, it is "ward-detainee," and if you look again at the next page, it again, with a dash, under number 3, under number 4, it is again "wards-detainees," "wards-detainees," "wards-detainees." On the next page, again, and that makes me very happy, and I take great pride in this, that there are regularly -- that the preventive medical measures are regularly enforced and that the medical supplies are much better than before, and that additional quantities of the necessary medical supplies have been received from the International Red Cross. So it is "ward-detainee" throughout the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So Witness, can we understand that you don't know whether there is any difference between "ward" and "detainee"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was no difference from my aspect, and what the military bodies did or meant, you maybe know but I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Judge Clark, I hope this answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think the witness has done his best. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could you have a look now at Exhibit P698.1, which is a report on the Heliodrom? And again, can I ask you is this a report that you drafted and is it your signature at the last page of the report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: This is my signature. I always sign my name in the same manner, so whenever you need my signature, it's very easy to recognise. This is about Heliodrom, nine pages, and I can see the names of Dr. Pero Maric, is a person who was a member of the main medical corps, Dr. Bozic and Dr. Nedjelko Hadzic, who was a Bosniak physician in Heliodrom. So this is about Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. And finally, and I will commence with a few more questions on that after you again confirmed the authenticity of Exhibit P686.2. This exhibit is a chart. And my question again is, Witness, did you draw up this chart and is it your signature on the bottom of the chart?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: If you have seen my signature so far, then it is clear to you that this is my document, but this table, I did it for myself. It shouldn't appear anywhere. It must have been stolen from me because this drawing I used when I went to see Dr. Bagaric, to discuss some things with him. I don't think this drawing should not be publicly exposed. Somebody must have taken it from my documentation. I may bore you when I say that I knew that this would happen and I wanted some things to be documented and presented to people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But, Witness, you confirm that you draw up this chart, and can I ask you that the conclusions that you draw in this chart, are these based on the reports which you just -- which were just shown to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Mostly yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And if a similar chart would have been made in the summer of 1993 - because this chart was drawn up in -- on the 24th of November, 1993 - would there be a great difference on the assessments on the various conditions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a table that gives just the aggregate figures. It doesn't show any dates. It is just my overall view of the problem. You know what the cumulation of data is. I write a lot and I accumulate data. So this was not a status presence. It was not the present state. It was just an overview up to then of what should be done, where should this be done and when. And some things may have improved but this is just a general view. It is just a cross-section, a general view of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, if you say that some things may have improved, let's focus on the Heliodrom. You were shown before an exhibit P618, which was an earlier report on the Heliodrom. Now, if you look at this chart, would the proposed measures in your first report on the Heliodrom of the 30th of September, would those measures have been included in your assessment on the Heliodrom in November, at the end of November, 1993? In other words, any of the measures that you proposed in your first report in September, would these measures have already been taken and would the conditions in the Heliodrom in November have been better than in September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes. For example, medical care, health care, in the report that I drafted in September, it says, under 2, under the proposed measures, it says, "Set up the hospital in the centre." This was true at the time. Moreover, under 3, "In the hospital, follow hospital principles, principles of work in the hospital," and this was what was done. Under item 4, when we did set up the hospital, all the serious patients were transported there to the war hospital by the car that belonged to the unit. We had problems there because Heliodrom was on the front line. Many were afraid that the car, while taking the patients to the hospital, may become the target, and that that could result in a number of wounded. As far as the cleaning of the perimeter is concerned, that is under 5, in Heliodrom, disinfection, under disinfection, there were three --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you specific questions on this table, item by item, so maybe you're getting ahead of us. Let me ask you another question first. Besides the four detention centres which you reported on, on this list, it says also -- it mentioned Duvno and Prozor, but there is no assessment on the condition of these two centres. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: You see, in the war, there are -- there is a lot of information but also a lot of misinformation. Dr. Bagaric and I learned that in these two towns, there were centres. Dr. Bagaric wrote to the commander of the area asking him to state whether there was a detention centre there. The answer came that there was none. I personally went to the chief of medical staff in Duvno, that is in Tomislavgrad, Dr. Peric. I also went to Prozor and I was told that these centres did not exist. I wrote this and Dr. Bagaric raised this issue. To this very day, I don't have any clearer information and I don't think that there were any centres there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, we heard evidence from several witnesses about two other camps which are not mentioned here, which is the Vojno camp and the Dretelj camp. Have you ever heard of these two detention centres, the Vojno and Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I heard of Dretelj, and as for Vojno, this is the first time I hear this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So let's focus, then, on Dretelj. You've said you've heard about the Dretelj camp. Why isn't Dretelj on this chart?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: This was November 1993, the end of November 1993, and I believe that Dretelj stopped existing long before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Fair enough. But if you look, then, at Rakitno and Dobrkovici, those two camps are mentioned, and there it says "does not exist any more." Why, then, not Dretelj and a line does not exist any more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: For a very simple reason. If Dobrkovici, the camp existed for two or three days, not more, and I was called there personally. Dr. Bagaric ordered me to go there and tell my colleagues in Siroki Brijeg what should be done. A few days later this camp stopped existing. What happened to the people, where they were taken, I don't know to this very day. The same is true of Rakitno, which was -- if there was any optimum humanity that could be achieved anywhere, that was in Rakitno. This also lasted for a short time. I'm sure you have reports on Rakitno. And I believe that this could be an example of how things should be done if they need to be done. So Rakitno could be a good example of how things are done. As a military physician, when I was reading about camps and I was -- when I was watching the movie Bridge on the River Kwai, I found it appalling. Rakitno could be the pride of a higher civilisation, such as Sweden and others, not to mention the country as primitive as ours. So Rakitno could be a good example.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd now like to go over with you the various conditions mentioned in the top row, and I'll start with the potable water. And I want you to focus only on Heliodrom. Let's leave the other camps aside. You rate the potable water at the Heliodrom as good. Now, let me first ask you: Did this condition improve? Was the potable water the same in the summer of 1993 and in November of 1993, or did the condition actually improve with regard to the water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sure you are not familiar with the situation with water in Mostar. The water supply was compromised, and for a long time there was no water in the town of Mostar. Personally, in my building, I had to go to a nearby well to get water, and it took me about an hour to fill a 20-litre bucket. So the situation with water was impossible at the time. Later on, I repeat, as a military person, I knew that in Heliodrom there was a water supply facility which used to be used by the former JNA. I knew that there was an aluminum-producing facility and another well. And owing to that, and having been an authority in military matters, I managed to put these two sources of water in use, and that's how Heliodrom was supplied with water. Another thing. I believe that you know that Heliodrom is supplied with water from town. My personal order was that in one point -- and in Heliodrom, chlorine in water was controlled three times, and this was done. And there is another order issued by Dr. Bagaric which said that the ABC unit was also supposed to control the water, and that also that the medical staff in the unit should also control water. Because you will allow that epidemics very often arise from the water, from the contaminated water, not only in wartime, but also in peacetime. Napoleon lost Egypt due to this, and when the medical --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm going to interrupt you. I'm really going to request you to be a bit shorter with your answers. Your answers have been very elaborated and we're getting a little bit in time constraints if you keep giving these long answers. Let me ask you one thing about what you've just said. You said that you managed to put some of the sources of water in use at the Heliodrom. When did you actually manage to do this? And I'm asking for a time period. Was this in the autumn? Do you recall the month when this actually -- when you managed to do this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in June or July. I apologise, Your Honours, but I believe you have to know the situation. Thirty per cent of the water in town was lost because the pipes were broken, and the epidemics could be broken not only in Heliodrom but also in town itself. Allow me to say that I know some things in the area of medicine, and I have to give you some elaborate answer so that you don't ask of some other witnesses the same questions, because I consider myself to be an expert in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know how much water a prisoner at the Heliodrom would get per day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact quantity, but you have to know that there were water cuts in town as well, due to the losses, and that the concentration of chlorine in the water was not 0.1 or 0.2, but -- which would be normal; it was 0.4, 0.5. I don't know about the quantities. I myself did not have enough water. I would very often reek of sweat because I did not have enough water to wash myself. And don't misunderstand me. Don't get me wrong. My wife also did not have water to wash herself. So what could we do? It was war. We could not wash ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So am I correct if you say here that you -- if you label water as being good, you're talking more about the quality of water rather than the quantity of water? Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I was talking about both, about both the quantity and the quality of water. But this is a cumulative report. On the 10th of May or on the 11th of May, it was not so. It was much worse. But later on things did improve. When you draw a table, you can't come up with an ideal table. I wanted to draw a table that everybody could understand, even those people who never were members of medical units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to the next item, alimentation. Now, again you label it as good. But in your report on the Heliodrom, which is Exhibit P698.1, you're rather critical on this aspect, on the alimentation, and you conclude that there's insufficient quantity and variety of food; isn't that correct? If you want to look at the report again, it's Exhibit 698.1. Witness, if you look at the report and look at the proposed measures under item 2, there are a number of measures which you propose with regard to the food. Isn't it fair that if you report -- it's making -- requesting all these measures, that it's a bit strange that you would label the alimentation as being good at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing: I told you that this table was cumulative. But you are just -- you're putting things out of their context. And it surprises me that you didn't see this, that on page 2, third paragraph, all the requirements of the medical and supply services have been attained. All the people were checked for epidemics. The control samples were preserved. The DDD measures were carried out permanently. There was a regular control by the medical and supplies services. And then there is also -- the food eaten by everybody is the same. The wards, inmates who were there and who were in contact with the food were -- had been examined. I think that this is an example of how things should be done. So some of them are today my friends. People who worked there were happy for working there. As for prevention measures, let me tell you that my standards were always higher. I thought that if my report portrays things in a somewhat worse light, then there is more room for improvement. As for the food, I was hungry for a time. My children were hungry. We didn't have the money. So you have to be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, can I take you to the top of page 6 of your report, and it's in the English on page 4, and it's the last paragraph before it starts with the proposed measures. And I'll read that paragraph out to you: "By a random sampling method, it was established that about 85 per cent of the wards were undernourished, the average loss of body weight being about 15 kilogrammes. It was observed that the wards assigned to physical labour were mostly of normal weight because of increased food."

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: What page is it on the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Page 6 on the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you conclude that the average loss of body weight for 85 per cent of the detainees was about 15 kilogrammes, is it then fair to label alimentation as being good?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where is this?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I have given him -- okay. Found it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P698.1, page 6 on the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, he has it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, have you read the paragraph? Do you have the paragraph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: [Inaudible]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, my question is -- my question is: How can you label alimentation as being good if the average loss of weight of the detainees was about 15 kilogrammes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: In that period I weighed 67 kilogrammes, and now I weigh 79. That's number 1. Number 2: You can see on the item 2 that we tried engaging all the international institutions, starting with the International Red Cross and others, to help us with the aliment. You can see here it says that there are two meals a day and that the third meal is being introduced. Nobody weighed these people before. They must have lost weight. It's indisputable, for various reasons. One of them was insufficient food, and the second reason was physical conditions. Detainees or people who are confined to a certain area are often known to lose weight. But let me stress again: I always overstressed some things in order to appeal to military, political, international organisations. I was not interested in this or that or the other. The only concern I had was how to help people. But again I repeat that everybody in Heliodrom ate the same food, across the board, inmates and their guards alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could you look at the paragraph above that paragraph which I just read out to you, and it uses the term -- it says the following: "We should stress once again that the above breakdown of medical conditions was put together by doctors who are in preventive isolation." Now, in several of your reports you use the term "preventive isolation." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I'll tell you -- I'll illustrate you that by my own example. In August 1991 I educated Muslim physicians, Bosniaks, my friends. I educated them and taught them things that I learned in the army. And as I was crossing the old bridge, there was a military point there manned by the BH Army, and a fellow citizen of Mostar told me, "Don't go to the other side. In Mostar, nobody is going to do you any harm, because we know you as an honest person, as a good person. But there are a lot of refugees from Gacko and Nevesinje, and as soon as they see you wearing your uniform they will consider you a potential enemy." So what is the meaning of this word "preventive"? I experienced several such incidents, and after that, when I say "preventive isolation," that is prevention against retaliation. If somebody is killed, if somebody is -- if somebody's property is stolen, I do not justify it as isolation. This was to help people, because some people did not have highly sophisticated consciousness. Some people did not kill for -- they killed for different reasons, and that is what I meant under the word "preventive isolation," and that's how I was explained that word by Dr. Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So detainees who were there under preventive isolation, they were actually there for their own good; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: These were doctors. A doctor is never an inmate, a detainee. A doctor is a doctor, protected by all international conventions, and no matter which side they belong to, they have to treat people, to put their medical knowledge to a good use. For example, Dr. Stranjak could go home whenever he wanted to go home. Dr. Hadzic, for example, he wanted to be affiliated with the army. Before that he was the doctor, the physician, of the Veles football club. His father was affiliated with the former UDBA. Maybe somebody, an extremist, would have killed him for stupid reasons, and I'm afraid something like that may have happened. Whenever Dr. Hadzic wanted to leave the camp, he could, and he indeed did, eventually, when he wanted to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I have a few more questions on that last paragraph, when it says: "It was observed that the wards assigned to physical labour were mostly of normal weight because of increased food." Did you know that wards were taken out for physical labour?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: What page is that on?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's on the same page, page number 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never saw that. I heard that some were taken. Personally, I said to my colleague, "Bozic, try to prevent this. It's a war crime." I asked where these people were. I met some people, and maybe for fear, or for other reasons, they told me they didn't go there. Some kept quiet, and from that I understood that they were taken there. What they did, I don't know, but later on I heard that they had been digging trenches or what have you. At that moment, I didn't have any personal knowledge, but I know that I told Dr. Bagaric that these people, if they existed, if they were taken for labour, that they had to be protected, because they were a product of a misunderstanding, and that was the worst form of maltreatment and harassment. If you have to do something against your better judgement, then that is the worst form of harassment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, the fact that prisoners who were assigned to physical labour were given more food, did it have anything to do with the fact that the HVO wanted these prisoners to be stronger, to be fit to perform labour, and is it in fact true that the prisoners remained in detention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the question is speculation. A speculation in the question asks for speculation in the answer. We heard that a minute ago. Just a moment, (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that the answer is quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please. I apologise. Can we redact this? Because I may have revealed the identity of the witness. Witness, we have to be careful. I just said one sentence or one word, but we have to be careful, I remind you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will redact that word. And Mr. Bos, I think the answer is quite obvious. There is no need to pursue it in that direction. It is time for a break, and we will break now and we will resume at 2.30 this afternoon. I hope you could finish your cross examination as soon as possible, as we resume this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, although I am a bit -- I have difficulties, given the long answers of the witness. I fully expected to finish by now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course. We will rise until 2.30 this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.03 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness NU, I have a couple more questions to ask you about the two documents which you had in front of you before the break, which is the table, Exhibit P686.2, and your report on the Heliodrom, Exhibit P698.1.
