So I would ask the registry to provide you with these two exhibits again, if you don't already have them. Witness, going back to the table, could you take the table in front of you again? Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you have five conditions, and I'll mention them: the clothing and the footwear, the heating and the hot water, the personal hygiene, the accommodation and the sanitation, which you labeled as being as does not satisfy. Now, my question is what does it mean when you say that these conditions do not satisfy? Does that mean that they don't satisfy the standards of conditions required by international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that this witness is not qualified to answer this. It would be -- it should be answered by people who are familiar with international law, international humanitarian law. I believe the witness has repeatedly answered this question, at least in his view, that is he has already answered it to the best of his ability. This question requires the answer by a legal expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we understand that this report was filed by the witness himself and in this report he says it is not satisfactory for the conditions. I think the Prosecutor is just asking a question to this witness to explain the meaning of why he says so in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and if I may add, he testified that he actually lectured on international humanitarian law at the Heliodrom. So I think he must have had some knowledge about the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will see what the witness will tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could you find, please, my report number 01-90/93 of the 20th of July, 1993, in which -- from which you can see the signatures of Mr. Bozic, and you can see that at that moment, so I repeat the 20th of July, 1993, when the inspection was carried out in the presence of Mr. Bozic, Dr. Hadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And we could not hear the rest of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, when to anyone in the Zagreb school or in London, in somewhere, we would find at least six cases of scabies, which means that the personal hygiene was much better, and I have already told you that I deliberately, on purpose, consciously, exaggerated things because I wanted to accord them more weight. Perhaps I might call to account to it, but I hoped that in this way these matters would be given attention and solved. In other words, I wanted to provide the maximum possible conditions. If that figure says 2.100 people, and I won't go into that, we've already talked about it, how can you then discuss six cases of scabies?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry. I'm looking for this report. I see the date is the 20th of July, 1993, and I do not know whether it was an oversight, but I have not received this report. I do not have a single report dated the 20th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, neither did I submit any report of that date. I'm also a bit at a loss to which document the witness has actually been referring. So maybe the court deputy could assist and tell us which document the witness is looking at.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm checking now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, certainly we don't have that report at our hands at this moment. But Mr. Bos, you may ask some questions around this line to make things more clear for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: On this report of the 10th [sic] of July, Your Honours? Because ... Actually, yes. What I would like to know from the witness:

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, which report are you referring to when you were mentioning a report dated July 1993? And maybe the court deputy could assist you and give the exhibit number of this report.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I am -- actually, I'm looking at the document. It is from his documentation, and I told him ... [inaudible].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the interpreters can barely understand what the registrar is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, you would have to repeat what you were saying, because we couldn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There are interruptions and it is very difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: How about now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: This is much better, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay. The witness has brought his documentation, and I told him he is not allowed to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, the witness is looking at his own documentation, which is not the documentation which we provided to the witness, not one of the exhibits, but his own documentation?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, I have no idea what document he's looking at, because it's his own document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you may re-ask your question before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So Witness, let --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I can tell you, though, that it's a stamped document signed by Stanko Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The thing is, if we don't have this document here in Court, it's very difficult to discuss this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I understand you have personal notes in front of you and you brought your own documents, but we cannot use those documents in these proceedings because we do not have those documents here and they're not admitted as exhibits. So I would like you to take away those documents and focus on the exhibits which we have provided you, the Prosecution exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I've explained that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the period of time that has elapsed is very long. I have told you that I knew that this time would come, and I've kept all the documents. You have a selection of documents. I know nothing about them. But allow me. This document is just as valid as any other, because it was signed by Mr. Bozic. On the other hand, this is a document with a stamp, a document which says what was done and what was found, and that is the answer to the question about the personal hygiene. This document shows how strict I was, how much I exaggerated things in order to improve the conditions. Because if you find only six cases of scabies, that is nothing. These are sporadic cases. And at the same time, Your Honours, it says, and you probably know, even know it, even though you do not have an adequate medical knowledge, just as I do not have a legal education, that the scabies is transferred by -- transmitted by contact and poor accommodation, which means that the accommodation was not all that bad or else we would have more scabies cases. I thought that you had all the documents, and I'd like you to have them, because then it would be much better. Because I also want the truth. But at any rate, thank you very much for having me here, and I wish that some day all of us, with our full names, bear our full responsibility. And thank you very much that in my country, in the name of the dead, in the name of the killed, in the name of the wounded, the truth will eventually surface. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I understand that your answer is that you exaggerated things in order to improve the conditions. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes. You are absolutely right. And thank you for understanding me so well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, if that's your answer, who did you issue this table to? If you say you exaggerated your assessments, for whom did you exaggerate this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I think we lost connection or something, because the image is fixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe the telephone line is cut off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we have the connection back. You may proceed, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, it appears that you can hear us but we cannot hear you. Can you say something again so that we can pick up your voice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I can hear you very well. And how you hear me, well, you know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, we hear you now. Thank you. Let me just ask you one question about the medical care which you've labeled as "very good" in the table, and I'd like to you look at your report again on the Heliodrom, exhibit P698.1 and look at page number 5, English page number 4. You have that in front of you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, there is a whole list of detainees grouped into various -- well, grouped into various diseases that they suffer. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: What page is that on in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: That's the B/C/S page number 5; in English, page number 3 and page number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, fifth on the bottom of that list, you indicate that there were 55 wards recovering from wounds. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you inquire how these people got wounded or injured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you look at this list, you can see at the bottom that it was established on the basis of case histories, that is on the basis of what the patient said, from people who naturally did not have adequate documentation and therefore everything would be taken with a reservation. But will you please look at page 4? Owing to the dedicated work, no incidents have been proven and nothing could be done that would affect adversely the health of the wards. That is, nothing could happen that would produce an adverse effect on them. On the other hand, if we look at the hygienic situation, the epidemiological situation on the bottom of page 4, the last passage says that only sporadic cases were recorded without any epidemiological causal chain. That is, Dr. Hadzic and all the Croats who worked there and all of us worked so well there that there wasn't even a theoretical possibility of an epidemic breaking out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, isn't it true that these 55 wards who were recovering from wounds were injured at the confrontation line while performing forced labour outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I hear that from you. I am not in possession of that information. This is the first time I hear this. But allow me, Your Honour, and Your Honours, look, see, we've even drawn up a list so that we could monitor the state of health. Commissions were set up. And on page 4, it says that these people - the passage, the fourth passage on page 4 - that they were being sent to the regional hospital in Mostar and that a maximum use of the medical supply and transports, and then in the war hospital, after that, the Heliodrom. That is, we even set up a commission to have these people treated without delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, were there any women at the Heliodrom? Female detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I did not see them but I heard there were about a dozen women, and one of Dr. Bagaric's orders was that women - although once again I say I'm not legally educated; women can also commit crimes - women below the age of 18 and over the age of 60, all severely ill, all those who need care, hospital care, should be released immediately. If you look at the diagnosis, the lumbago, if you look at them, there are ten of them, and I'm also suffering from it and it almost happened that I couldn't be here but I realised how important it was for me to be at the Tribunal and therefore, I came. You see, even Mr. Krsnik does not have documents because I did not give them because all I care about is the truth regardless of what it is, but the truth that will help you and that will help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to show you one more exhibit and then we are done. And I'd like Madam Registrar to provide you Exhibit P630.2.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've seen something very important on page 4, on page 4 of this document, if I may. There is a regular --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: The one that we've just been talking about. I mean it is very important for you. It is very important for you to know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Allow me, page 4, in English --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? I think --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Yes, of course, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I think the Defence counsel can come back to that in redirect on this issue. So the Defence counsel will ask you to clarify whatever you want to clarify in redirect. I'd like you now to move to Exhibit P630.2. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, and you can glance through it but let me tell you this is a letter from Mr. Stanko Bozic addressed to the President, Mr. Mate Boban, and it's dated the 10th of October, 1993, and in this letter, Mr. Bozic expresses his concerns about numerous problems at the Heliodrom. And I'd like you to direct your particular attention to item number 2, which is the English page number 2 and B/C/S page number 2 as well. You have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Isn't it correct here that Mr. Bozic, under item 2, actually describes several problem areas regarding the medical care at the Heliodrom which you had assessed as being "very good" a few weeks earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I can gather, this document was sent only to Mr. Boban because it is addressed to him only. That is, neither Dr. Bagaric nor I could have this document, and therefore I cannot say anything about it objectively speaking, but I'll nevertheless try to answer your question. Item 2 under A, incorrect, because undoubtedly I was informed, and I went there, and my colleagues, fellow physicians, they always told me that we sent an ambulance whenever somebody needed to be taken to the hospital. Item B is absolutely inaccurate, it's completely wrong, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We could not get a part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: In case of the medicines, if there were no medicines available in the warehouse, then the hospital didn't have them and the Heliodrom doesn't have it. The in-patient unit was set up and there were beds there and all that, so that I definitely do not understand this because I absolutely stand by what I just said, that item B is inaccurate. It could have happened, for instance, at some particular point in time that there would be no medicines, but we were getting medicines from Croatia. I had the preventive medicines in sufficient quantities. Whenever I needed them I got them. So I do not know what this is. Perhaps somebody is washing his hands because of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, if I can address your attention to item 1. Isn't it correct that Mr. Bozic here reports on detainees still being taken out for forced labour? And we're talking about October 1993. And isn't it true that detainees were still taken out of the Heliodrom, notwithstanding any concerns expressed by the Red Cross, in August 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Your Honours, how could I know that? I don't know. You say that this was happening, but I don't know it. If Bozic has written that, then it is his moral responsibility. I don't know. And please do not think that I do, as a doctor. How could I know that? This is terrible. When I hear that somebody is harassed, maltreated, that is a terrible thing for me. If somebody is taken for forced labour, I find it terrible. I didn't know anything about that. How could I have known? If this was true, then I'm ashamed as a former member of the HVO. I'm ashamed as a human being, as a doctor. It was no accident that I was chosen a member of the presidency of the infectologists of the world, because I think that morale and morality is my forte, my brightish side. So if this is true, then I'm ashamed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, finally, Witness, could you look at the top page of this document, the first page. There's something which is handwritten around the name of Mr. Mate Boban, and isn't it true that Boban made a personal note to Mr. Valentin Coric, which is his handwritten note, in which he underlines the seriousness of the problem, to sort the matter out within the limits of what is possible and the requirements of humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have not intervened too much. We don't know whether this report was written by Mr. Bozic. This is what my learned friend claims. We don't know whether this is handwriting of Mr. Boban. This is my learned friend claiming. And the answer to all these questions is: How on Earth could my witness know all these things? He was in no position to know all that. And my learned friend has already heard answers regarding this document. The witness has on several occasions answered his questions, and the answer was that he is seeing the document for the first time and that he has no knowledge whatsoever about any of these things, and my witness has repeated that on several occasions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't matter that we hear the answer from this witness once again. Mr. Bos, would you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can wrap up, and I'll just put my last question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, isn't it true that following the months that the Red Cross actually visited the Heliodrom in August 1992, the conditions in the Heliodrom hardly improved, and that by the time of October 1993 the conditions were still not up to the standards of international humanitarian law? Witness, did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: No. No. There was no link. There was a break in the link, so I couldn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: But I can answer your first question, if you wish me to do so, the question regarding Mr. Mate Boban. Sir, I have never --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I have one more question to ask you. Just listen to this question and respond to that question and then our cross-examination will be over. Is it not true that in the months following the visit of the Red Cross at the Heliodrom in August 1993 that the conditions at the Heliodrom, or any other camp, hardly improved and that the conditions of confinement in these camps never, ever complied with the norms of the international community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have my documents. I have it with me. Your registrar can see those documents, and in these documents she can see that on the 11th of May we took all the measures in Heliodrom, when I was invited there, and we did our best to adhere to the humanitarian law and all the Geneva Conventions. I did not even know whether the Red Cross came or didn't come, but I know that I worked all the time, that my first concern was for the people, how to prevent illnesses among them, how to remain their friend. And I believe that with time, the quality of the work improved. My colleagues, who started by being totally ignorant, not through their own fault, they finally learned a lot of things in order to prevent things from happening. And if these -- so it is not the International Red Cross or any other institution that dictated my work. It was my own consciousness, my obligation as doctor, not the International Red Cross, and I would like to reject all your insinuations in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Re-examination, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Just one or two things I need to clarify for your benefit. My learned friend has given me the opportunity to ask a question. 698.1 is the exhibit that I would kindly ask the registrar to put in front of the witness, 698.1/4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Page 4. Sorry. The interpreter apologises

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: 698.1, page 4. Can you please tell us what you wanted to say about this document. That's page 4 in B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, it seems that the connection is okay. Would you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would kindly ask Madam Registrar to put Exhibit 698.1 in front of you, and can you please look at page 4. This is the page that you wanted to read to us, i.e. that you wanted to comment upon it, that is, document 698.1.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I would like to refer to the last passage, which is very important from the point of view of prevention of contagious diseases, which in these circumstances would have been the most difficult segment of medicine. I'm proud that even under such difficult conditions, we had permanent screening of patients - when I say "patients," I mean people who were there, patients - for scabies, pediculosis, diarrhoea, enzymatic diseases, because at any -- at no point in time we registered any of these diseases. However, this didn't -- doesn't mean that they could -- that these diseases couldn't break out at any given time. The order issued by Dr. Bagaric said that the concern for detainees was a permanent concern. He ordered us to protect our image as doctors, as human beings, and if I can say something else --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, go on. We are not finished yet. I have some things that I need to clarify which according to my mind require additional clarification. Can we now ask Madam Registrar to put document P565.4 in front of you? Do you have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Not yet. Yes. This is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you please read the second passage slowly and tell me where is it that this document says that there were 2100 detainees in Heliodrom? This is what the Prosecution claims, and can you please find the place where it says so? Does it say so anywhere? Is that -- does that refer to the present number of detainees or of some future number of detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: No. What it says here is that the commanders of the 3rd Brigade verbally informed us that they were not in a position to provide food for 2.000 detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Does it say anywhere that at any present moment there were 2100 detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: No, it doesn't say so. It just says that the verbally we were informed by these people that they were not in a position to provide or assure food for 2000 people. I don't know, Mr. Krsnik, what you are implying here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That is because I did not want to object during cross-examination, but what I'm implying is that in this document it doesn't say that there were 2100 detainees at Heliodrom at any given point in time. Let's move on, Witness. There is one more thing that I would like to discuss with you. Where does it say, in which document - I believe that when I'm asking this question, I'm referring to document P698.1 - English version, page 4 - page 6. Can you please read once again the first passage on page 6 and tell me where does it say that the detainees who worked outside received special food or that they received more food than any other detainee in Heliodrom? Where does it say so? What does it say exactly? When talking about detainees, does it say where they worked, for how long? The document speaks for itself. However, my learned friend put some leading questions during his cross-examination, and I'm not allowed to do that in my re-examination or my examination.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: If you are referring to the first passage, it says here that it has been noticed that detainees who were assigned to physical labour were mostly of normal weight because of increased food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Does it say anywhere in the document who gave them more food and where were they assigned to physical labour? Did they have to go outside or were they working within the Heliodrom perimeter? My learned friend asked you this. He said they were -- they received special food in Heliodrom, those detainees who allegedly were assigned to forced labour, according to him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Personally, I believe that the Prosecutor did not have all the medical documents. Maybe he could have consulted me. I would have given it to him, because I know that we, in one of Dr. Bagaric's orders, read that we had to do the screening of the weight of those persons who, for one reason or another, were losing weight, and that they -- their food had to be improved. So it very often happened that some detainees received more and better food than even army members, but rest assured that reinforced food was given only to such people who were losing weight. But also rest assured that there was no way I could know that somebody was taken away for forced labour and that for that reason they received more food or better food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you now explain to the Honourable Court how is it possible that your table, for which you said that it may have been stolen, when you sent any of your reports, did you put the name of the addressee on top of that report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: If you look at my reports, I would also -- I would always indicate the addressee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you ever send this table to anybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: No. Personally, I can't remember but I think that only Bagaric had a copy of that table, because, you know, (redacted) are very sensitive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I'm sorry we have some technical problems. You answered that, "No. Personally I can't remember but I think that only Bagaric had a copy of that table, because, you know, (redacted) (redacted) are very sensitive." Then you were cut off. Would you please continue your answer to this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said "sensitive," I meant that I always exaggerated things in my reports and I wanted Dr. Bagaric to know everything. On the other hand, you can't achieve things without being really perseverant [sic]. I'm sure you have many of my reports, and I always pointed out that this involved a lot of stress. I did this table with my own hand, wanted to show it to Bagaric, and I showed it to him. I even gave it to him. How this reached you, I don't know, because obviously it wasn't addressed to anybody. It wasn't addressed to anybody else. I'm glad you have it, because it shows what conditions we worked under. We had to exaggerate things. I'm sorry, I'm finding this very difficult. I can't help shedding a tear. I just wanted to point out that we worked as human beings, and that's why sometimes we had to exaggerate things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, my last question to you: Your documentation that you have, as you can see, you have been provided with only four or five documents signed by you. We don't know how many of such documents does the Prosecution have. They have only provided us with these four or five. However, the documentation that you have, would you be willing to provide it to us on our request?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I may be invited to this Court again. I would like to keep this documentation, although it testifies to a very difficult period of my time, but also the period of time that I am proud of. I don't want to give these documents to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Maybe just photocopies for us to translate and for us to have an integral picture.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, sometimes when I'm alone by myself during the night, when my family is asleep, I go through these documents, and I don't want to leave it to you. I want to be able to live with my memories contained in these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Fine. Listen, it might be of assistance to us, so that I will ask you, although you have not shown it to me, to show these documents to me. I hope that you will find enough goodwill to give these documents to me and then we shall have it translated, if need be. But thank you very much, Witness. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Questions from the Judges. Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, first of all I want to thank you very much for coming and making yourself available to the Tribunal, in spite of the fact that you have a very painful back condition, and I want you to know that when I ask you these questions, that I have taken very careful note of what you have said about how alien the concept of war is to a person who is trained to providing care for all ill people, without discriminating between their allegiances and their political affiliations. I accept all that and I've taken very careful note of what you say about the superhuman efforts that you have gone to, and obviously you've been successful in achieving and preventing a severe epidemic in the town of Mostar or in the Heliodrom. Now, you can take it that I've listened very carefully to that. Nevertheless, I have a number of questions for you, sir. You said at the beginning of your evidence that when you were with the HVO, that your expertise was in demand and that you therefore were on call at the hospital, but you weren't there very frequently. Can I ask you where you were when you were not at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Clark, I wore the uniform, as a man who is a member of the main medical staff, and I therefore had to make rounds of the territory called Herceg-Bosna, all of it, in order to prevent any epidemics from breaking out. And please don't misunderstand me. I'm one of the few people who treat contagious diseases, but I also learned about the prevention in the army. In the former Yugoslavia, you do not know people who are familiar both with the prophylactic measures and the treatment. I'm one of those few, because I passed my major's test, so I had to go through the hospital to see what was the situation in the infectious ward, because there were only four doctors. Otherwise I travelled all the time around, went to Livno, to other places, merely with a view to preventing any epidemics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. And what I'm trying to understand from you is: Was is your duty exclusively to prevent disease, or were you also responsible in some way for the well-being of the prisoners at the various camps? In other words, the conditions under which they were held, were they something that you were involved with or were you uniquely involved in the prevention of infectious diseases?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: My only responsibility was the prevention of infectious diseases. However, I have quite a lot of seniority behind me, and I'm a man who treats people. That is my vocation. And yet in war we had young doctors who were still not aware of that. So it was natural for me to train them, just as I now teach other students. So my only job was the prevention. But at the same time I was engaged in training. That was not based on any orders. I did it on my own, because I knew that knowledge had no frontiers and that knowledge shouldn't be only mine, that I should transmit it and impart it to somebody else. Because in that way I also preserve myself. I knew if they don't know how to do something, they will be calling me, so that I will be involved again, and I therefore thought I should train them, train other people. I think that the person who can receive, absorb the knowledge is happy, but even happier is the one who can impart his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. So can I take it from that that your primary interest and responsibility was, no matter where you went in Herceg-Bosna, to prevent disease and to educate other doctors and paramedics in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Clark, my primary responsibility and the reason for my appointment was to prevent infectious diseases. All the rest I did additionally and on my own. You know, I've seen a lot of the world. I'm a member of numerous international organisations, so on and so forth, and I am also a member of the faculty. And nobody told me, but Bagaric once said, "Well, when you can show them." And even if he hadn't told me that, I would have shown them, because I think that the one who learns will help the man, because their knowledge should serve hope. And I am a big adversary of ignorance, you know, a major foe of ignorance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That's good to know. What I'm leading on to, then, with further questions is: As you had a specific and obviously very large area of responsibility, who in fact was the medical officer who was primarily in charge of the well-being and health of the prisoners? Who would have been the doctor who would have determined the policies at the Heliodrom and Ljubuski? They're the camps that we're interested in.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Well, you see, when people find themselves in a situation like that one, like the Heliodrom, the international conventions also say that these men may not be under the control of units or individuals, but only under the armed force. All the rest is contrary to humaneness. So the control was carried out by physicians. The service was headed by Dr. Bagaric, and the specific executors, when it comes to Heliodrom, were doctors Dr. Hadzic and Dr. Stranjak and doctors who were serving with the home guard units, such as Dr. Pinjuh, Dr. Pehar, and a number of others, and they were to do that. And I was to give them guidance, to give them instructions how to prevent diseases. But since I was a military doctor -- and I've also passed the test for a major. It's a very difficult test, much more difficult than the specialistic one. So that the doctrinary views, to my mind -- for instance, every wound is infected unless proven to the contrary. So I will always give tetanus. My colleagues, for instance, didn't know it. And again, any water, until we proved that it is chlorinated, is contaminated, and that is why I ordered that the chlorine content ought to be 0.4. I know that it should be 0.2, because just to be on the safe side. And I would do the same thing again. But you have to know these things. You cannot fight against something unless you know it. But this knowledge I acquired in the JNA. That was not something that I was taught at the university.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I'm taking a long time to follow through with my questions from your answers, but what I wanted to know is: As you had a very large and specialised interest, but a unique interest, would it be fair to say that you wouldn't have been the appropriate medical person to in fact inspect all the facilities and conditions under which prisoners were held at the Heliodrom or Ljubuski? I know that we're moving on with time, Doctor, so we have to have answers that are a little more succinct. I hope you don't think I'm being rude.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I didn't hear. I couldn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, doctor, I was saying that I notice that it's 20 to 4.00 now and time is moving on and I have a few more questions to ask you, so we have to be a little more succinct, and I didn't want you to take offence from that remark. What I wanted to know is, as you had a very specialised area of interest and expertise, can I take it that you were not the actual expert who carried out a full assessment of Ljubuski and the Heliodrom in relation to the conditions under which prisoners were held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: You want me to answer this? Your Honour Judge Clark, I personally went to see those people, those wards, because my colleagues would take me there. It would be either Mr. Bozic or Dr. Tomic who would take me along. I was familiar enough, but a large number of things, taking people for forced labour and so on and so forth, I really knew nothing about it. Yes, there was talk but I did not see it. I do know, though, that that part of the preventive medicine was done exactly as it is envisaged by the postulates of the military wartime epidemiology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I do not doubt that, sir, but were you aware or did you personally see that any prisoners were held in solitary confinement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Clark, rest assured that I do not know. Maybe there were some. I'm not denying it. But they did not take me there. My colleagues, and at times Mr. Bozic, took me along, but I do not know that. I am not saying that there weren't because maybe they existed but I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I accept that totally. We have just heard over the months some fairly harrowing evidence, from two people in particular who were held allegedly for a very long time in what were described as fairly appalling conditions, but you don't know anything about that, you can't help us in any way. Can I -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour Judge Clark -- yes, yes, of course, do go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I didn't really want an answer, sir, because I felt that your response was valid, that these things could have happened or they may not have happened but you know nothing about it, and I would not disagree with what you're saying. I was wondering if you ever noted personally injuries as opposed to illness on detainees which would have been, from a medical point of view, inconsistent with good humanitarian management.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Clark, according to my documentation from May 1993 -- of May 1993, it says here -- it mentioned here places that I visited, and it also says here that the detainees, the wards, said they had no problems relative to harassment and that they were full of praise for the guards, although I have it recorded somewhere. I cannot really say that there were not such cases, but I'm telling you I went there with my colleagues and I never saw any such case, and I give you my word of honour. Had I seen it, I would have informed Bagaric, because I think that it would be -- I think that it is inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are afraid we missed part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could not get the whole answer. We did not hear the answer. He said something, "informed Dr. Bagaric," and then about 30 seconds were lost. We could not hear it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I would have certainly informed Dr. Bagaric, and personally I would have taken my utmost that such a person, be it even my brother, be punished because nobody has the right to take another man's life. I'm sorry that all this has been selected. You should have seen it. When I wrote such reports, I was afraid that I would also become a victim, fall victim to one of the extremists, but here certain things are presented out of context. Well, you know, when Richelieu said, "Well, give me anybody's letter and let me take something out of context and I will cut his head off," so please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I hope, sir, that you're not equating us with that sentiment expressed by Richelieu. I wanted to ask you in conclusion about the report of the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: May I say something, Your Honour? Judge Clark, may I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I take pride in being here today, and I'm aware that you were brought there by your ethical and professional reference. It wasn't a state that brought you. And I hope that my answers and my dialogue with you will help you in your work, and that is why I wish to express my thanks to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I have one last question, which might be a difficult one for you. I'm referring to your report which is called Exhibit 698.1, and perhaps if the Registrar would kindly assist you or assist me by putting that report in front of you, and I want to refer specifically to the very last paragraph of your conclusion. Have you found it, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: In this report, there is a reference to quite a number of medical conditions among the prisoners, and then there is a reference to 55 wards recovering from wounds. Now, Mr. Bos the Prosecutor asked you about this, and you appeared to minimise the veracity or authenticity or reliability of that assessment on the basis that it was made by doctors who were apparently in isolation, and in fact, you appeared to repeat the final paragraph of your assessment. Can you explain to me why the fact that the assessments were prepared by medical practitioners who were prisoners would affect its validity? Why would the fact that they were prisoners make their assessment unreliable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Judge Clark, unfortunately you are wrong. Not once does it say so anywhere. In here it says they -- that they did not have adequate medical documentation. For instance, among the diseases, it is mentioned that -- one can see that there are two with some problem or that there are seven with eye anomalies, what kind of -- seven wards with -- so there was no dilemma. My colleagues did not have adequate documentation, and had I been there, they would have said the same thing, that without documentation, everything is probable or supposed, and just look, Judge Clark, at the conclusion that you are talking about, and I will read it out. May I, with your permission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: "In spite of all the listed shortcomings, the medical epidemiological situation is very satisfactory, as infectious and contagious skin diseases are present only in sporadic form without any epidemic relationship. The sporadic appearance of these diseases is quite normal in these locations, in such locations." And then the penultimate passage, "The inspection established that there was no ill treatment of wards." I hope I've answered your question, at least in part, if not fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The question that I really wanted you to address was the one that was posed by Mr. Bos in relation to the 55 wards who were described as recovering from wounds. As a non-doctor and as a lay person, it would still seem to me that one doesn't have to have documentation in order to make an assessment that somebody is recovering from a wound. And why, then, is my question, why, then, did you minimise the accuracy or appear to minimise the accuracy of that finding because the doctors who made the finding were in fact not at liberty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Allow me to repeat it once again. Far be it from me to minimise it and -- because they are my colleagues, but the condition after the wounding, one can be -- if you are hit by a bullet or something, then you're finished, but it can be a muscle injury which doesn't take more than five or six days, but for these five or six days you must be spared work or whatever. And without medical documentation, allow me, if you now went to a doctor here in the -- there in The Hague, without any documentation, do you think you'd be believed? I wouldn't believe you, and I do not think that my colleagues in The Hague would believe you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I see. My final question -- well, maybe I have two questions. Can you tell me how those -- your colleagues who were held against their will in the Heliodrom, how they were actually housed? Were the doctors and the nurses who were described in one of the reports in a separate unit from the prisoners or did they find themselves in the same rooms with mattresses on the floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: It is only natural for the doctor to be in the infirmary, which is open around the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is did those doctors and nurses who assisted in the care of the prisoners, did they have any special treatment or were they treated in the same way as the other detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry. I just wanted to know - perhaps you don't know this - whether the doctors and nurses who were detainees and who assisted in the care of their co-prisoners, did they share the same accommodation as the other prisoners, or did they have special privileges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Two doctors. One worked in the infirmary which worked around the clock, and of course he was accommodated there. The second doctor was in the in-patient unit, and naturally he was accommodated there. It would be very wrong for you to look for a doctor anywhere. For instance, the doctors from the units who were there, they were also accommodated in the in-patient hospital for those soldiers, not with the others. Because after all, doctors are protected persons. They are protected so they can place their knowledge in the service of others and to help them. That was my order, because if a doctor is there, then he can help, and he is duty-bound to be at a place -- at the location where a medical institution is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I once again express my appreciation for your assistance? Especially considering your back condition. I hope I haven't added to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge's questions? Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It seems to me that there is one thing which warrants clarification because I'm afraid there is a misunderstanding and I will try to ask -- to rephrase Judge Clark's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In relation to these a 55 wards and the documentation, is it that they had -- that they said that they had been wounded but did not say when and produced documentation about their wounding, or were they wounded after having been put at the Heliodrom? I don't know how else to say it. And they brought the documentation and told these doctors, "Well, we were wounded over there and here is documentation," or were they wounded at the time when you wrote the report? Because that is the fundamental question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I object. This is a leading question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it is a leading question, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Your Honours, I don't really have a problem because that is why we can't clarify certain things. I'm quite clear what this report is about. The Prosecutor asked questions about this and Her Honour asked this and I was trying to rephrase it, but I think that the meaning is absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You do not have to rephrase Judge Clark's questions, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. My question -- my question -- let me try to reword my question. It is quite logical. This is the Tribunal which cares about the truth rather than if I went wrong and I will ask my question properly. So my question, the sense of my question, the meaning of my question is whether these people were wounded whilst at the Heliodrom. That's the question because it is very important to learn where they were wounded and when and whether the doctor knows that or whether they were wounded two years before that and then produced the documentation. That is why the documents were not trusted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So, Doctor, were they wounded whilst at the Heliodrom? Witness, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, you see, in this last paragraph, it says they did not have with them adequate and proper medical documentation. Had they been wounded whilst at the Heliodrom, they would have unquestionably ended up in the War Hospital, because the Heliodrom did not have the facilities for the extension of that kind of medical help and we would be deluding ourselves. Now I will use a military medical term. There are different degrees of emergency. Wounding is of the first order of emergency, and this, the treatment is usually provided by a surgeon. There was no surgeon at the Heliodrom. So had he been wounded at the Heliodrom, he wouldn't be there. He would be somewhere in the surgical ward of the hospital or where he would have been operated on. Or if it was a serious wounding, then he would have been taken to Split. With all due respect to my colleagues, they simply -- at the Heliodrom they were not qualified enough to do that kind of intervention, but I wish to thank them, to extend my heartfelt thanks to them for what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to give your testimony. We all wish you good luck in the future. The court deputy will show you out of that room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage are there any documents to tender, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The Prosecution have six new exhibits to tender: Exhibit P686.2, which is the table; Exhibit P698.1, which is the report by this witness on the Heliodrom; Exhibit P699.1, which is his report on Gabela; Exhibit P700.2, which is the witness's report on Livno; Exhibit P702.2, which is the witness's report on Ljubuski; and finally, Exhibit P565.04, which is the letter of Mr. Bozic addressed to Mr. Stojic, dated 14 August 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course what the witness has said, that these reports were his, he owned up to them, so I have no grounds for objections. As for the others, this one is admitted. Well, 630.2 [as interpreted], unfortunately, has already been admitted, so that I can't object to that one either. What I want to clear up now, Your Honour, is the source of documents. Although the witness said that the signature was his, and so on and so forth, these are not the originals. They must be copies. And I still claim before this high -- the first world tribunal that the source of these documents is not the Croatian government, because the Croatian government cannot be the source of these documents, because surely the Croatian government did not collect the documents of the medical corps of a third country and it could not be in the possession of them and it cannot have them now. So we want to know which is the true source, for two reasons: so that we can look at them and check the authenticity of these documents, and so the Defence could apply for these same documents from that same source. The complete documentation. Now, it is interesting. All of a sudden documents are now emerging with the indication of a source of the Croatian government. Well, excuse me. That is my government, so I will immediately write to the Croatian government and to ask them to make their archives accessible to me, because they've obviously opened their archives to the Prosecution but not to me. I am not aware at all of these documents of the Croatian government, and we hear that this is the archives of the Croatian government. I do not think they have them, but when it says here "the Croatian government," it really sounds pretty curious and we'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Since Mr. Krsnik raised that question, Mr. Bos, are you in a position to answer it at this moment or give us some explanations about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I can't be more specific than what's indicated here, that we got these documents from the Croatian government, and we got numerous documents from the Croatian government, and these were included in here. And I think the witness has sufficiently authenticated the documents, and I really don't see why we need to discuss where these documents are coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, oh, yes, it is very important to discuss it, although the documents authenticated four documents. I don't know about others. I don't know how many. I want to know who, the first name and the last name, which ministry, which agency, who gave those documents to you. It couldn't have been the Croatian government, because the Defence also has the right to turn to the same source. Your Honours, we must enjoy the same rights as the Prosecutor, and now they are hiding their sources so that we cannot gain access to them. So who is it who said that he was the Croatian government? I'm telling you that it was not the Croatian governments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can perhaps try to offer a solution, or at least some additional information, because it may in fact just be an issue of the nomenclature that's been used on this particular document. Throughout the trial we have distinguished between records or documents obtained from the Zagreb archive, what we've called the Zagreb archive, which this Trial Chamber heard considerable testimony about from Mr. Prelec during the Prosecution case in chief. This is a place where Prosecution staff have gone, and I must take issue with the comment made by counsel. It is an archive that's open to not only the Prosecution but to the Defence. Any number of Defence investigators and staff, from any number of cases in this Tribunal, can be seen and found working in this archive, and I have reason to believe that investigators working for counsel are also taking advantage of that archive. But that's the Zagreb archive, and I think we tried to be consistent throughout in identifying documents coming from that archive. Now, apart from the archive, there have been documents which we have obtained from the Croatian government which are in evidence, and I have in mind a series of documents that relates to events involving Robert Nosic, for example. That's the HVO gentleman who was abducted from the HVO military police station in Mostar in November of 1993. That's a series of documents that was obtained from the Croatian government pursuant to a request for assistance that this office issued to the Croatian government actually before the archive even became available to us. Going back to the very first day of this trial, the Trial Chamber may recall the testimony of OTP investigator Jan Van Hecke, who testified about these various categories of documents. So as I stand before the Tribunal, or the Trial Chamber, at this moment I can't tell you or counsel whether this particular series of documents denominated "Croatian government" are in fact from the archive or whether they were obtained pursuant to a request for assistance. I can offer to find that information and provide it to the Trial Chamber if you ask us to do so, but I think I would certainly what Mr. Bos has said, which is that with respect to these four exhibits, the witness very clearly authenticated them. He verified that they are in fact documents that he made. So it's not clear to us why, really, it's necessary to do anything more concerning their authenticity or admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stringer. And you have said that you'll do something else to help us to find the source of those documents at a later stage. We are very glad to hear that. We believe that it will be a great help to the Defence counsel for their documentation. As for the six sets of the documents used during the cross-examination, we believe that the witness himself authenticated those documents already, which is sufficient. So these six documents are admitted into the evidence at this stage. So we'll break now at this moment, and tomorrow morning, at 9.30, we'll continue with the next videolink witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of August, 2002, at 9.30 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
